holding: Silent on concurrency. Time for employer events (8.4), time without money for some neutral events such as epidemic (8.4(d)), and a 28-day notice condition for claims (20.1).

Where an employer event and a contractor cause delay together, the contractor gets time for the period of delay caused by the employer event. The contractor's own concurrent delay is no answer to the extension.
pinpoint: Dyson J at [13], quoted in Walter Lilly [367] and Adyard [276]

holding: An employer event that has no effect on the completion date earns no extension. Real concurrency needs both causes to delay the works.
pinpoint: HHJ Seymour QC at [31], quoted in Adyard [278] and Saga [242]

holding: First edition of the Delay and Disruption Protocol. A broad view of concurrency: delays whose effects are felt at the same time.
Apportionment of loss between causes in global claims, which laid the ground for City Inn.
pinpoint: Lord Macfadyen at [36], quoted in Walter Lilly [480]

holding: With no dominant cause, a fair and reasonable extension may apportion the concurrent delay. Nine weeks awarded.

Majority: delay is a matter of common sense; a critical path analysis is not essential; a dominant cause governs; otherwise apportion. Lord Carloway dissented and would look at the relevant event in isolation.
General rule: where delay is concurrent, the contractor gets an extension but cannot recover loss it would have suffered anyway.

Concurrency only if both events in fact delay the works and their delaying effect is felt at the same time. Notional delay is not enough. The employer's change caused no actual delay to a project already in critical delay, so no extension.
rule: actual delay, felt at the same time

holding: City Inn apportionment is inapplicable in England. Where a Relevant Event is an effective cause, the contractor gets a full extension.
Follows Adyard. There must be a concurrency actually affecting the completion date as then scheduled. Owner delays inside the yard's own delay did not count.
True concurrency is rare. Time and money are treated separately, and compensation follows only separable employer delay. Guidance, not law (Thomas Barnes [109]).
Compensation events are assessed prospectively against the programme at the time. Time and money go together.
Concurrency is to be assessed under rules in the Special Provisions. If none are stated, as appropriate in all the circumstances.
A clause saying concurrent delay earns no extension is enforceable. The prevention principle can be displaced by agreement. The position under unamended JCT is 'not entirely free from doubt'.
Time where the event is an effective cause; money only on a but-for basis. Concurrent roof and steel delays: 119 days' extension, 27 days' prolongation.
Still no express concurrency term in the standard form, per commentary, so the Cyden question is left to bespoke amendment.
